To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the prevalence of pressure ulcers was 1.3% in the study sample, 2) the prevalence of severe pressure ulcers was less than 0.5% in the study population, and 3) the most important risk factor for the development of pressure ulcers in the study population was the presence of medical conditions.
the risk factors for pressure ulcer development in the outpatient setting are the same as those in the inpatient setting.
the prevalence of PU is 1.8% in the outpatient setting.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the relationship between the development of pressure ulcers in the community and the risk factors associated with this condition.
the development and evaluation of a novel method for the detection and quantification of pressure ulcers in a clinical setting.
the identification of risk factors for pressure ulcer development in an outpatient setting and the development of a prediction model for pressure ulcer development.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is a strong evidence for a causal association between the use of pressure-reducing devices and the risk of pressure ulcer development.
the most important medical risk factor for pressure ulcers is a combination of a low level of consciousness, a low level of mobility, a high level of dependency and the presence of a pressure ulcer.
the risk factors associated with pressure ulcer development are age (older), gender (female), comorbidity, immobility, malnutrition, incontinence and poor tissue perfusion.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown that medical conditions can be used to identify patients at risk of pressure ulcers in the outpatient setting.
the use of the 2nd generation of the Pressure Ulcer Scale for Healing (PUSH) is recommended for use in research and clinical practice.
we have developed a new method for the identification of risk factors for pressure ulcer development in a large outpatient cohort.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of the NPUAP Pressure Injury Staging Tool is not recommended in clinical practice, as it is not valid for use in the acute care setting.
